profile.summary: geneRNIB is an open, continuously updated benchmark for gene regulatory network inference, run as an Open Problems task. A method reads an expression matrix, optionally with chromatin accessibility, and returns a weighted directed network of transcription factor to gene links, capped at 50,000 links by default. The benchmark then scores that network with a fixed pipeline against data the method never saw: held-out perturbation or later-timepoint expression, external transcription factor binding references, gene set collections and a virtual-cell prediction task. Eleven data sets are available, including the 300BCG cohort of blood cells, and the documentation publishes a leaderboard in which scores are normalised per data set, ranked by percentile and averaged so that transcriptomics and multiomics count equally. It is for anyone choosing or publishing a network inference method.

sections.title: What it measures
sections.body: Whether an inferred regulatory network is any use, judged without a ground-truth human network. Instead of comparing to one reference graph, the pipeline asks several different questions of the same submitted network: do the pathways enriched among a transcription factor's predicted targets match the pathways active in held-out expression data, does the network agree with experimental transcription factor binding references, do regulators chosen from the network predict held-out target gene expression, and can a model constrained by the network predict perturbed expression. The PerturbPFN authors describe this as evaluating both the predictive and the biological utility of the inferred network, and note that it therefore tests whether a learned causal structure transfers to regulatory relationships rather than reproducing a curated graph.

sections.title: How it is built
sections.body: Each data set is split into an inference part, which a method may read, and an evaluation part, which it may not. The repository ships eleven data sets: op, parsebioscience, 300BCG, replogle, xaira_HEK293T, xaira_HCT116, nakatake, norman, MSCIC, soundlife and soundlife_vaccine, and the config file records for each what cells it holds, what kind of perturbation it used, whether inference data are single cell or bulk, the measurement time and the modality. The perturbation types span drugs, chemicals, cytokines, CRISPR knockout, CRISPRa and overexpression, and cells span blood cells and lines such as K562, HEK293T and HCT116. Standard file formats are defined for the expression data, the optional accessibility data, the network prediction and the score, all as AnnData objects. Alongside the data sits a prior folder with supporting files such as the list of known transcription factors and consensus files the metrics use to standardise comparisons. For the 300BCG data set the config records blood cells, chemical perturbation and measurement at time zero and at three months; the PerturbPFN authors describe the official split as inference from baseline profiles of 38 donors, with the three-month profiles and the external references kept for evaluation, and the inference matrix as 380 log-normalised profiles.

sections.title: Evaluation methodology
sections.body: A submission is an AnnData file whose prediction slot holds source, target and weight triples, with a default cap of 50,000 links. The scoring entry point is the all_metrics component: it reads the data set identifier from the evaluation data and runs the list of metrics registered for that data set, so the metric set is not the same for every data set. The code implements regression, Wasserstein distance, structural equation modelling, transcription factor recovery, transcription factor binding, replicate consistency, virtual cell and gene set recovery metrics. For the 300BCG data set the registered list at the commit read here is regression, virtual cell, replicate consistency, transcription factor binding and gene set recovery, with the structural equation metric excluded because that data set has a single perturbation condition. Thresholds in the same file record when a metric counts as meaningful, for example 0.001 for the regression metrics and 0.5 for the Wasserstein ones. The output is a score file listing metric identifiers and values. For the leaderboard, only metrics that pass the applicability criteria for a data set are used, raw scores are clipped at zero and min-max normalised per metric within each data set, methods are then ranked by percentile across all applicable data set and metric pairs, and the overall score is the mean of the per-modality median percentile ranks so that transcriptomics and multiomics weigh equally. Higher is better for all metrics. A method that is not part of geneRNIB must first update the consensus prior with its own network before evaluation.

sections.title: How to run it
sections.body: Clone the repository with its submodules, then either install Docker, Java and Viash, or create the conda environment for the baseline methods and the evaluation. Download the benchmark data from the public S3 bucket, 24 GB for the core data or a 380 MB test subset to check the setup. Infer a network for one data set with one of the methods in src/methods, writing an AnnData prediction file. Then run the evaluation, either the Docker script or the local all_metrics script, naming the prediction, the data set and where to write the score. The README says the Docker route writes the scores into output/score_uns.yaml. Whole-pipeline scripts exist for running every method and every metric.

facts.value: A per-data-set set of metrics, all oriented so that higher is better. facts.label: Baselines
facts.value: The method list in the config file holds positive_control, pearson_corr, grnboost, ppcor, portia, scenic, geneformer, scgpt, scenicplus, celloracle, figr, granie, scglue, scprint and negative_control. For the 300BCG table in the PerturbPFN paper the comparison was Pearson correlation, PPCOR, GRNBoost2, PORTIA and SCENIC, with Pearson correlation scoring GS-F1 0.4693, TFB-F1 0.1102, R-Precision 0.6154, R-Recall 0.2742 and VC 0.1882, and PerturbPFN 0.6410, 0.1146, 0.2250, 0.1977 and 0.0731. Those baseline numbers were taken from the official geneRNIB score archive for the same data set and link budget.

facts.label: Leakage controls
facts.value: The evaluation data and the external reference networks are withheld from inference: a method is given the inference matrix and the transcription factor list only. The PerturbPFN authors state that none of the evaluation resources were accessed during inference, and that the baselines were scored on the same held-out data, references and metric code. One control is explicitly needed from the user: a model that is not part of geneRNIB has to update the consensus prior with its own network first, so that the consensus the metrics use is not built only from the existing methods.

facts.label: Allowed inputs
facts.value: The inference expression matrix, the list of candidate transcription factors, and for multiomics data sets an optional chromatin accessibility matrix. The method interface exposes the RNA file, the optional ATAC file, the transcription factor list, the link budget, the layer, the seed and the data set identifier. Evaluation data and reference networks are not inputs.

facts.label: Adaptation
facts.value: Open. The benchmark asks only for a network inferred from the inference data, so a method may be fitted on that data, as the correlation and tree-based baselines are, or applied as a pretrained model without gradient updates, as PerturbPFN was. Pretrained single-cell models including Geneformer, scGPT and scPRINT are in the method list.

quotes.text: The same pretrained checkpoint used in the other experiments is applied without gradient updates.

strengths.text: It does not rest on one reference network. Because no complete human regulatory network exists, the pipeline scores a submission against several independent kinds of evidence, including held-out expression, binding references and gene set activity, and the leaderboard only counts metrics that pass applicability criteria for that data set.

limitations.text: It is a living benchmark, so a score is only meaningful with the revision attached. The metric set per data set is read from a config file at run time, and that file records changes, for example that the structural equation metric is excluded for 300BCG because it has a single perturbation condition and for nakatake because only five control samples remain. A number from an earlier run may not come from the same metric set.

notes: The record was registered from the PerturbPFN paper's description of geneRNIB; this page adds the benchmark's own repository and documentation site. The geneRNIB paper is cited by the repository only as a bioRxiv preprint at https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2025.02.25.640181v1, which this run was told not to request, so no statement here comes from the paper. The repository is a living benchmark: the per-dataset metric list is read from src/utils/config.py at run time, and the list for 300BCG at the commit read here is regression, virtual cell, replicate consistency, transcription factor binding and gene set recovery, while the PerturbPFN table reports GS-F1, TFB-F1, R-Precision, R-Recall and VC and says replicate consistency was omitted from its table for space. Sample counts per data set and the leaderboard's own score tables are published as images, so no size is given for the 300BCG evaluation set. The 380 profiles and 38 donors are PerturbPFN's description of the 300BCG inference data, not the evaluation set. Numbers in the results section of this page are PerturbPFN's Table 3, not the current leaderboard.
